title: The Elements of Tāna
summary: Lists the eleven elements of tāna, from skipping and turning back to mixed tempos and repetition, with examples. Then extending a pattern through all notes (tables in Rūpak, Dādrā, Kaharvā, Tīntāl), ālāpa and Sa as its resting point, vādī–saṃvādī, four kinds of pause, and five actions of elaboration.

blocks.text: Now, the elements of tāna

When I have to build tānas (fast melodic runs) in a particular rāga, I have to maintain the qualities of the rāga and their jātis (classes by number of notes). In such a situation it is difficult to carry through alaṅkāras (patterned exercises). To get over this difficulty, [we] attend to the subtle elements within the alaṅkāras, and carry those same elements through in the tānas.

blocks.verse:
लंघो निर्वर्तो बार्धक्यं पक्षैक परिपक्वता।
राग वाचक पुष्टिश्च गमकाश्च विविधास्मृताः।१०८।
blocks.text: Laṅgha (skipping), nivarta (turning back), bārdhakya (gradual expansion), pakṣaika-paripakvatā (strengthening one side), rāga-vācaka-puṣṭi (reinforcing the rāga's identifying phrase), and gamakas (ornamental oscillations), held to be of various kinds;

blocks.verse:
अन्यारम्भः समाप्तिश्च लयानाम् मिश्रणं तथा।
वक्रताऽ वृत्तयश्चैते गुणा स्त्वेकादशस्मृताः।१०९।
blocks.text: anyārambha (beginning on a different note), samāpti (ending [on a different note]), likewise the mixing of layas (tempos), vakratā (crooked movement) and āvṛttis (repetitions): these are held to be the eleven qualities.

That is, from a practical point of view there are eleven main qualities used in tānas (fast melodic runs). And by mixing any two or three of these, many more qualities can arise; all of them are tāna-tattvas (elements of tāna). These qualities are described below with examples.
1 - Laṅghana (skipping)
Laṅghana (skipping) is used in ascent or descent in two ways. One is on its own, as in (Sa Ga Re Ma Ga Pa); the other mixed with alaṅghana (not skipping), as in (SaRe SaGa ReGa ReMa)
2 - Nivartana (turning back)

The literal meaning of nivartana is 'returning'. When, before the ascent is completed, some part of the descent is mixed in and then the ascent is made again, this action is called nivartana (turning back). For example (Sa Re Ga Re Sa Re Ga Ga)
3 - (Bārdhakya) Baṛhat (gradual expansion)

In this action too nivartana (turning back) is necessary, but in it one has to return again and again to a fixed place and then advance regularly one note at a time; so it has an existence somewhat different from nivartana. For example - (Sa Re Sa, Sa Re Ga Re Sa, Sa Re Ga Ma Ga Re Sa, Sa Re GaMa Ma Pa Ma Ga Re Sa). In this way the group of notes keeps growing, step after step.
4 - Pakṣaika paripakvatā (strengthening one side)

It means strengthening one of the two sides, ascent or descent, in many ways. It is a more suitable action mostly for rāgas of the auḍava-sampūrṇa jāti (five notes in ascent, all seven in descent), as in Bihāg - ( Ga Re Sa, Ma Ga Re Sa, Pa Ma′ Ga Ma Ga Re Sa, Ni Dha Pa Ma Ga Re Sa)
5 - Rāga-vācaka puṣṭi (reinforcing the rāga's identifying phrase)

That is, presenting the group of notes by which the rāga becomes clearer, beginning it from different notes. This action is mostly used in saṅkīrṇa (mixed) rāgas. For example - to keep Rāmkalī apart from Bhairav -- Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa komal Re Ga Ma Pa Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa, Ṡa Ni komal Dha! Pa Ma′ Pa komal Dha komal Ni komal Dha Pa Ma Pa Ga Ma Ga komal Re Sa. Or, in a song, bringing out any one of these four aspects, words, sargam, notes and tāla (metric cycle), is also an example of it.
6 - Gamaka

This is a celebrated action, whose description is given in other treatises too. My view does not differ from theirs. (svarasya kampo gamakaḥ) That is, the use of shaken notes is called gamaka (ornamental oscillation). Performers use various kinds of gamaka with their skill, which are impossible to write down; but the ordinary gamaka, in which the sparśa (touch) note predominates, is like this: ( Sa Re SaGa ReGa Re Sa Re Ga ReMa GaMa Ga Re Sa). If the sparśa note is taken out of this, it will become merely an example of ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition).
7 - Anyārambha (beginning on a different note)
Its meaning is to begin from one note after another and end on one [note], for example - (in Yaman - Ṇi Re Ga, ḌhaṆi Re Ga, Ma′ Ga Re Ga, Ni Dha Pa Ma′ Ga Re Ga)
8 - Anya samāpti (ending on a different note)
Beginning from one note and ending on other notes, changing each time. For example - in Yaman Ṇi Re Ga, Ṇi Re Ga Ma′ Pa, Ṇi Re Ma′ Dha Ni, Ni Dha Pa Ma′ Ga Re Sa).
9 - Layānām miśraṇam (mixing tempos)

When a tāna (fast melodic run) is flowing in one laya (tempo) and suddenly, leaving that laya, its double or half laya is mixed in momentarily, again and again, we may call this action miśralaya (mixed tempo). Only accomplished sādhakas (practitioners) can do this. In it, the blending of many layas is more interesting, as, in Rāga Yaman itself - Ṇi ReRe Ga Ma′ - DhaPa Ma′ Ga Ma′ Ma′Dha -Dha Ni Dha NiNi Dha Pa - DhaDha Pa Ma′ Ga -- Ma′Ma′ Dha Ni Ṡa NiDha Pa Ma′Ga ReGa -Re Sa.
10 - Vakratā (crooked movement)

This action is useful for vakra (crooked) rāgas. For example GaRe MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa Ma′ Ga PaRe Sa, Ma′ Ga PaMa′ DhaPa NiDha Ṡa, and so on. 'In rāgas such as Gauṛ Sāraṅg - MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa Ma′Ga PaRe Sa. MaGa PaMa′ DhaPa NiDha Ṡa
11 - Āvṛtti (repetition)

It is mainly of three kinds, as in GaGa ReRe SaSa NiNiNi Re Re Re Ga. This we call ekāvṛtti (one-note repetition). And ṠaNiDha ṠaNiDha PaMa′Ga PaMa′Ga - this we call trayāvṛtti (three-note repetition). Repetition of more notes than this can indeed be done, but in practice it is not suitable from the point of view of beauty.

Besides the above 11 actions there are some more actions too, such as 'miśra saptaka' (mixed octave), that is, saying the same group of notes in two octaves, as in Ga Re Sa, Ġa Ṙe Ṡa. But for fear of enlarging the book, more actions are not being mentioned.

blocks.verse:
स्वरद्वयम् प्रकल्प्याथ त्रयम् वा तु चतुष्टयम्।
स्वकल्पित क्रमेणैव समुदायम् प्रकल्पयेत्।११०।
blocks.text: Having set up two notes, or three, or four, one should form a samudāya (group of notes) in an order of one's own devising.

That is, taking two notes, or more, three or four notes, and carrying through the elements above in them, the sādhaka (practitioner) should compose samudāyas (groups of notes) of various orders on the basis of his own imagination.

blocks.verse:
तस्य क्रमस्य निर्वाहो यदा सर्वत्र क्रीयते।
समात्रिक समूहेषु तदाऽलंकार कल्पना।१११।
blocks.text: When that order is carried through everywhere, in groups of equal mātrās (beats), then [there is] the making of an alaṅkāra (patterned exercise).

That is, if the order stated before is carried through, step by step, in the following notes, and those mātrās (beats) are also kept in mind, the alaṅkāra (patterned exercise) extends into a full ascending and descending form.

The point is that in the sādhanā (practice) of alaṅkāra one has to keep two kinds of order in mind - one is the order which you have made in two or three notes; the other is the general order of ascent and descent, which is fixed by the śāstra according to the rāga or thāṭ (parent scale). Suppose you composed this order "Sa Re Ga Re Sa" in three notes, which is in five mātrās (beats). If you carry this same order through Re Ga Ma in place of Sa Re Ga, then in place of Sa there will be Re, in place of Re Ga, and in place of Ga Ma, and the second link has formed like this: Re Ga Ma Ga Re. In the same way keep shifting each note forward until it ends on the Ṡa of the tāra saptaka (upper octave). Then, to come back from there, the same order has to be changed into its descending state. That is, the place that Re has in the ascent, Ni will have that same place in the descent. In this way the descending form of Sa Re Ga Re Sa will be Ṡa Ni Dha Ni Ṡa. Now if we want to play its full extension, we should first write it out as below and then play it. Doing so, we can gain an easy flow even in difficult alaṅkāras.

blocks.text: (The instruction is that) while writing, we went on writing the successive notes one below another, under each note, and while reading, went on reading from left to right. In this way both orders were carried through. To confirm the above, some alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) are being written. In these alaṅkāras, along with various elements and tālas (metric cycles), care has also been taken that they be practical. In these alaṅkāras some blank spaces are left for the sādhakas (practitioners). Fill them in and practise.

blocks.text: In the same way, in four notes too, other alaṅkāras (patterned exercises) can be composed in the form of a sūtra (formula) and spread across all the notes. For example - SaRe SaRe Sa Ga Re Ga SaRe SaRe SaMa SaMa GaMa| Sa ReRe SaRe GaGa Re Ga Sa Re Re Sa Re MaMa GaMa| Sa ReSa -Sa Re Sa GaGa Re Ga Sa ReSa Sa Re Sa MaMa GaMa, and so on.

blocks.verse:
वार्तालापस्तु भाषायाम् विलापो रोदने भवेत्।
संलापोऽभिनयादौ स्यात्तथाऽलापः स्वरेषु च।११२।
blocks.text: Vārtālāpa (conversation) belongs to language; vilāpa (lament) is in weeping; saṃlāpa (dialogue) is in acting and the like; and likewise ālāpa is in notes.

Bhāva (feeling) has existed ever since this world was created. Or say that creation itself is full of bhāva, and pralaya (dissolution) is its absence (abhāva). It became necessary for living beings to exchange feelings with one another. It is from just there that we must take the various languages and gestures to have arisen. Along with languages, nāda (sound), and along with gestures, laya (rhythm) arose naturally. When one being began to wish to nurture another, from then on lāpana (speaking) also became necessary. According to the grammar of Śrī Pāṇini, from the root pal comes lāp or pālana (nurturing), and from the root lap comes lāp or lāpana (speaking); these two roots became each other's avaroha (reversal). In the śloka above, the meanings of the root lap with prefixes, and their fields, are shown. If vārtālāpa (conversation) is suited to language, then in the same way vilāpa (lament) is suited to weeping, saṃlāpa (dialogue) to acting, and in the same way ālāpa to notes.

blocks.verse:
संसारस्थित जीवानाम् व्यवहाराय परस्परम्।
कल्पिता ब्रम्हणा ह्येते भावाभिव्याक्ति हेतवः।११३।
blocks.text: For the dealings of beings living in the world with one another, these were devised by Brahmā as the means of expressing bhāva (feeling).
That is, so that the beings in the world can deal with one another, Brahmā himself, through the Sāma Veda, created ālāpa and the like relating to music.

That is, each note has a particular relationship with another note. We may call it bhāva (feeling), and from the union of the bhāvas of several notes arises a rāga full of bhāva, which is delightful or rasa-enhancing for all beings in the world.

blocks.verse:
षण्णाम् स्वराणाम् जनकः षड्जाख्यः खरो मतः।
तेनैव भावस्य पूर्तिः स्याच्छब्दानाम् क्रियया यथा।११५।
blocks.text: The note called ṣaḍja is held to be the begetter of the six [other] notes. By it alone is the bhāva (feeling) completed, as [the sense of] words is by the verb.

When we accept some nāda (sound) as Sa, then the remaining notes have to be fixed on its basis. So the full name of Sa has been given as ṣaḍja, that is, the one that gives birth to the six. Just as in any language the sense of the other words depends on the verb, in the same way in music too the sense of all the notes is completed only on Sa. If one does not rest on Sa, the ālāpa will seem meaningless. Understood roughly, ālāpa or svara-vistāra (elaboration of notes) rests on just three main actions: movement in some notes, rest on some notes, and the full stop on Sa. Just as in conversation many pauses are expected, from the comma to the full stop, in the same way in ālāpa too there are four kinds of pause: nyāsa, apanyāsa, vinyāsa and sanyāsa. Human life too is furnished with movement and pauses. Although man projects only the bhāva (feeling) in his heart onto notes and tāla, and, seeing life as ascent, descent and sthāī (steady state), sees his own bhāva reflected in the mirror of the notes, still it is a practical truth that going from Sa to komal Re gives the feeling of karuṇa rasa (pathos), and going to śuddha Re gives the feeling of śānta rasa (calm). And on returning to Sa again, that feeling becomes more vivid, as it were, and makes its impression on the listeners. So the effect of all the notes is held to arise from Sa alone: the nearer a note is to Sa, the more bhāva it can bring out, and the effect of a note far from Sa grows faint. So to keep that effect fresh, Pañcama and Madhyama make the contribution of Sa itself. This is the meaning of the following śloka.

blocks.verse:
दूरवर्ति स्वरस्थानाम् भावानामनु भुतये।
पंचमस्तु सहायः स्यादभावे मध्यमः स्वरः।११६।
blocks.text: For the feelings of notes placed far away to be experienced, Pañcama is the helper; in its absence, the note Madhyama.

When we want to do svara-vistāra (elaboration of notes) or ālāpa in a rāga, it is first of all necessary for us to know the separate importance of the notes used in that rāga. Generally the importance of Sa is the same in all rāgas. It will be quite fitting if we regard it as the Mahārājā of the kingdom that is the rāga. After it, the second place has to be given to Pañcama, because it is Sa's helper, in the role of Prime Minister. If Pañcama is varjit (omitted) in that rāga, then in its absence Madhyama is accepted. After that, the vādī (principal note) and saṃvādī (consonant second note) of that rāga we can liken to the Governor and the Chief Minister. Then we give the other notes the place of ordinary subjects. Once such an arrangement is made, moving on the ordinary notes and stopping on the special notes: these are the only two actions we have to do. In moving, the use of tāna elements, and in stopping, a beautiful kampan (shake), will be graceful. In the ālāpa of a rāga my attitude will be that of a curious tourist in a particular city. That is, fixing one place for the night's stay, setting out each day for one important place, and coming back again to the fixed place. If on the way one has to stop a little for some special reason, one must stop only for a short time and keep one's destination in mind. At the destination, walking around and sitting in due manner will come naturally. If some things are left unseen at that place, one can set out for the same place again the next day too. So it is proved that pauses can be made in many ways.

blocks.verse:
षड्ज पञ्चम भावेन स्थितावन्यौ स्वराविह।
वादि संवादिनौ स्याताम् रागरूप विवर्तकौ।११७।
blocks.text: Two other notes standing here in the relation of ṣaḍja and pañcama would be the vādī and saṃvādī, which shape [and set apart] the form of the rāga.

That is, the two notes between which the ṣaḍja-pañcama relation exists are held to be the vādī (principal note) and saṃvādī (consonant second note) of one rāga or another. And by these alone being changed, rāgas with the same notes are also understood as different; for example, in Rāga Bhūpālī Ga and Dha are vādī and saṃvādī, and in Rāga Deśkār Dha is vādī and Ga saṃvādī.

blocks.verse:
न्यासापन्यास विन्यास सन्यासास्तु विरामकाः।
न्यूनाधिकम् महत्वं तु स्वराणां यैस्तु संभवः।११८।
blocks.text: Nyāsa, apanyāsa, vinyāsa and sanyāsa are the pauses, through which the greater or lesser importance of the notes comes about.

On the notes of greater or lesser importance in rāgas we use four kinds of pause. First, we play many note groups ending on the vādī (principal) note, one after another, and in each of those note groups we make an ordinary pause; this we call nyāsa (resting note). The slight short pause that we make on some other note in order to complete that nyāsa, we call upanyāsa. If within the nyāsa we utter a particular note group again and again and reinforce it in many ways, we call these pauses vinyāsa (varied rest), because variety and distinctiveness are both expressed by the prefix 'vi'. And when, after these nyāsas, we come to Sa and feel rest, this is called sanyāsa (final rest on Sa). For example, in Rāga Yaman, on the note Gāndhāra: Ni Re Ga, PaMa′ Ga, Re Ma′ Ga - these are nyāsas. And NiRe Ga ReGa Ma′ PaMa′ Ga, Ṇi Ḍha Ṇi Re Ma′ Ga, Ṇi Ṇi Re - Ṇi Ṇi Ga - - these are all vinyāsas endowed with the qualities of alaṅkāra; and ṆiRe GaMa′ Pa -- PaMa′ Ga: here, after making apanyāsa on Pañcama, the nyāsa of Ga took place. Then Ga Re -- ṆiRe Sa. Here, after making apanyāsa on Re, sanyāsa was made on Sa.

blocks.verse:
आंदोलन च वक्रत्वं अभ्यासः स्वर संगति।
विकर्षणं श्रुतीनां चेत्येते पंच किृया मताः।११९।
blocks.text: Āndolana (oscillation), vakratva (crookedness), abhyāsa (repetition), svara-saṅgati (association of notes) and vikarṣaṇa (pulling) of the śrutis: these are held to be the five actions.

In the svara-vistāra (elaboration of notes) of rāgas, five actions are done besides the tāna elements. Their names are given in the śloka above. 1 Āndolana (oscillation), that is, making the blowing breath tremble on the note on which one pauses. This āndolana is mostly done on the guitar. On the bansī (bamboo bānsurī) some people are not able to do it, because for that it is necessary for the sādhaka (practitioner) to practise bhastrikā prāṇāyāma (breath control) for 6 months in the winters. When we take the breath in and out quickly, just as a dog sits and pants in the hot days, that kind of practice is called bhastrikā prāṇāyāma. It should be done for two or three minutes every day. 2 Vakratva (crookedness): when we do not sound a note straight, but use it joined with the notes around it, we show a changed form, sometimes with one sparśa (touch) and sometimes with many sparśas, that is, in the form of mirkīs - this we call a saṃyukta svara (joined note) or vakra svara (crooked note). In other śāstras there is a somewhat different definition of vakra, but by that the crookedness of the rāga becomes clear, not that of the note. 3 Abhyāsa (repetition) means repeating the rāga-identifying note group. 4 Vikarṣaṇa (pulling) means drawing the śrutis in between, in the form of mīṇḍ (glide), to go from one note to another. 5 Svara-saṅgati (association of notes) means using, besides the vādī and saṃvādī, the association of some [other] notes that suits the rāga.

blocks.verse:
बहुधा बादिनि विन्यस्य गौणेऽपन्यास पूर्वकम्।
सन्यासः षड्जे कूर्याद्रागालापस्तदा भवेत्।१२०।
blocks.text: Placing vinyāsa many times on the vādī, after apanyāsa on the secondary [notes], one should make sanyāsa on ṣaḍja; then rāga-ālāpa comes about.

That is, after making apanyāsa (intermediate resting note) on the gauṇa (anuvādī, assonant) notes, making vinyāsa in many ways on the vādī (principal) note, and making sanyāsa on Sa: this is the meaning of rāgālāpa. Here it is necessary to show, with an example, the signs for nyāsa and the others.

The sign of ordinary nyāsa will be given as (+), in the form of a plus; the sign of vinyāsa as (,); the sign of apanyāsa as (-), in the form of a khaṇḍākār (fragment); and the sign of sanyāsa as (||), in the form of a full stop.
